宋.note:
In 960 Zhao Kuangyin seized the throne from the Later Zhou in the Chenqiao mutiny and made Kaifeng (the Eastern Capital) his capital, with Luoyang as the Western Capital, Yingtian Fu as the Southern Capital (1014) and Daming Fu as the Northern Capital (1042). The conquest of the Northern Han in 979 ended the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms; after the defeat at the Gaoliang River the Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun were never recovered.
Local administration was organized into circuits (fiscal-commissioner circuits): fifteen were fixed in Zhidao 3 (997), rising to twenty-three in the Yuanfeng era. Song made the Treaty of Chanyuan with Liao in 1004 and alternately fought and made peace with Western Xia; Emperor Shenzong backed Wang Anshi's New Policies (1069–1085), and Wang Shao opened up Xihe.
In 1125 the Jin armies came south; in the Jingkang Incident of 1127 the emperors Huizong and Qinzong were carried off north and the Northern Song fell. Zhao Gou took the throne at Yingtian Fu (the Southern Song), moved from place to place south of the Yangtze, settled the capital at Lin'an in 1138, and in 1141 made the Treaty of Shaoxing with Jin, with the border along the Huai River and Dasan Pass.
The later Longxing (1163) and Kaixi (1206) northern expeditions both failed. In 1234 Song joined the Mongols to destroy Jin, then failed in the Duanping campaign to retake Luoyang, and the Song–Mongol war lasted over forty years: Diaoyu Fortress checked Möngke (1259), and Xiangyang held out through a six-year siege (1268–1273). Lin'an surrendered to the Yuan in 1276; at the Battle of Yamen in 1279 Lu Xiufu leapt into the sea with the boy emperor on his back, and the Song came to an end.

辽.note:
Yelü Abaoji of the Khitans founded the state in 916 and built the Supreme Capital, Linhuang Fu, in 918. The state acquired the Sixteen Prefectures in 938 and took the dynastic name Great Liao in 947 (reverting to Khitan in 983 and becoming Liao again in 1066).
It ruled "each according to its customs": the Northern Administration governed the imperial camps and tribes, the Southern Administration the Chinese prefectures and counties. There were five capitals, each heading a circuit: the Supreme Capital Linhuang Fu, the Eastern Capital Liaoyang Fu, the Southern Capital Xijin Fu (Youzhou), the Central Capital Dading Fu (1007) and the Western Capital Datong Fu (1044).
Liao defeated Song at the Gaoliang River in 979 and at Qigou Pass in 986; in 1004 Empress Dowager Xiao and Emperor Shengzong marched south, and the Treaty of Chanyuan, made in the twelfth month of that year, brought annual payments of silver and silk from Song. Of three invasions of Goryeo, the one of 1019 ended in heavy defeat on the Cha and Tuo rivers (Gwiju). Liao twice invaded Western Xia, in 1044 and 1049.
Emperor Tianzuo was absorbed in hunting; the Jurchens rose in 1114 and routed him at Hubudagang in 1115. The Supreme Capital (1120), the Central Capital and Yanjing (1122) and the Western Capital fell one after another, and with Tianzuo's capture in 1125 the Liao came to an end. The imperial clansman Yelü Dashi went west and founded the Western Liao.

北辽.note: In 1122, after Emperor Tianzuo fled into the Jiashan hills, the imperial clansman Yelü Chun, custodian of Yanjing, was raised to the throne; historians call this the Northern Liao. Song attacked Yanjing twice that year and was beaten both times by Xiao Gan and Yelü Dashi. After Yelü Chun died of illness Empress Dowager Xiao ruled as regent; at the end of the year the Jin army came through Juyong Pass, Yanjing surrendered to Jin, and the Northern Liao ended.

西夏.note:
The Tuoba clan of the Tanguts had long held the four prefectures of Xia, Sui, Yin and You (the Dingnan Circuit). In 982 Li Jipeng surrendered the territory to Song, but his clansman Li Jiqian fled to Dijin Marsh to resist Song and took Lingzhou (Xiping Fu) in 1002. Jiqian's son Li Deming submitted to both Song and Liao, built up Xingzhou from 1020, and took Ganzhou in 1028.
Li Yuanhao succeeded in 1032, took Liangzhou, Guazhou and Shazhou, and in 1038 proclaimed himself emperor of a state called Great Xia, with its capital at Xingqing Fu. He defeated Song three times, at Sanchuankou (1040), Haoshuichuan (1041) and Dingchuan Fort (1042), made the Treaty of Qingli in 1044, and in the same year crushed Emperor Xingzong of Liao at the Battle of Hequ. He also created the Tangut script.
Xia and Song then fought back and forth along the Hengshan Range and the Tiandu Mountains: Song's five-pronged campaign against Xia (1081), the Battle of Yongle (1082) and the Battle of Pingxia (1098). After the rise of Jin, Xia submitted to Jin. From 1205 the Mongols attacked six times, besieged Zhongxing Fu in 1209, and destroyed the state in 1227.

金.note:
In 1115 Aguda of the Wanyan clan of the Wild Jurchens proclaimed himself emperor of the Great Jin, with his capital at Huining (the Supreme Capital). After crushing Liao at Hubudagang, Jin took the Eastern Capital Liaoyang Fu in 1116, made the Alliance Conducted at Sea with Song in 1120, and destroyed Liao in 1122–1125.
In 1125 Jin marched south in eastern and western columns and destroyed the Northern Song in the Jingkang Incident of 1127; it set up the client state of Qi (1130–1137). The Treaty of Shaoxing of 1141 fixed the border along the Huai River and Dasan Pass. Emperor Xizong and the Prince of Hailing (Wanyan Liang) adopted Chinese ways: Wanyan Liang moved the capital to Yanjing (Zhongdu) in 1153, invaded the south in 1161, failed at Caishi and was killed by his own officers. The reigns of Shizong and Zhangzong (1161–1208) were the height of Jin, and Shizong was hailed as "a little Yao or Shun"; the realm was divided into nineteen circuits.
Jin was crushed by the Mongols at Yehuling in 1211, moved the capital to Bianjing in 1214, and lost Zhongdu in 1215. In 1232 its main army was wiped out at Sanfengshan; Emperor Aizong fled to Guide and then Caizhou, and when the Song–Mongol allies stormed Caizhou in 1234 the Jin came to an end.

伪齐.note: In 1130 Jin made Liu Yu, a Song official who had surrendered, emperor of "Great Qi", first at Daming Fu and from 1132 at Bianjing, ruling Henan, Shandong and Shaanxi. Qi repeatedly helped Jin attack Song, but its invasions of 1134 and 1136 both failed (the Battle of Outang). In 1137 Jin deposed Liu Yu and Qi came to an end.

东夏.note: Puxian Wannu, Jin pacification commissioner for Liaodong, rebelled and declared his own state in 1215, first called Great Zhen and later Eastern Xia. It held what is now eastern Jilin, southeastern Heilongjiang and northeastern North Korea, with its capital at Nanjing (the Chengzishan mountain fortress at Yanji). It briefly submitted to the Mongols in 1216 but soon broke away again, and was destroyed by the Mongol prince Güyük in 1233.

西辽.note:
In 1124 the Liao imperial clansman Yelü Dashi led his followers west to Kedun City; in 1132 he proclaimed himself emperor (Gurkhan) at Emil, and in 1134 he occupied Balasagun and renamed it Quz Ordu as his capital. He defeated the Western Kara-Khanids at Khujand in 1137 and routed the Seljuk sultan Sanjar at Qatwan in 1141; Transoxiana, Khwarazm and the Uyghurs of Qocho all became tributaries. Historians also call the state the Qara Khitai.
It ruled through vassals: the Kara-Khanids, Khwarazm and the Qocho Uyghurs kept their own rulers and paid annual tribute. The Qocho Uyghurs went over to the Mongols in 1209 and Khwarazm broke away in 1210; in 1211 the Naiman prince Kuchlug usurped the throne, and in 1218 the state was destroyed by the Mongol general Jebe.

大蒙古国.note:
In 1206 Temüjin held a kurultai at the source of the Onon, took the title Genghis Khan, and founded the Great Mongol State (Yeke Mongol Ulus), organizing his people into units of a thousand households.
He invaded Western Xia six times between 1205 and 1227, attacked Jin from 1211 and took Zhongdu in 1215; in 1219–1225 he campaigned west against Khwarazm, while Jebe and Subutai pursued as far as the Kipchak Steppe. In 1227 Western Xia was destroyed and Genghis Khan died. Ögedei destroyed Jin in 1234, built Karakorum in 1235, and sent Batu on the western campaign of the eldest sons (1236–1242), which broke Rus', Poland and Hungary.
The sons received appanages: Jochi, Chagatai and Ögedei each had an ulus, while the youngest son, Tolui, kept the homeland. Möngke (1251–1259) sent Kublai to conquer Dali and Hulagu west (destroying the Nizaris and Baghdad), and died before Diaoyu Fortress in 1259. In 1260 Kublai and Ariq Böke fought over the succession, and the empire split into the Yuan and the four khanates.

元.note:
In 1260 Kublai took the throne as khan at Kaiping and proclaimed the reign title Zhongtong, then fought Ariq Böke for four years over the succession. Kaiping was raised to Shangdu (the Upper Capital) in 1263 and Yanjing renamed Zhongdu in 1264; in 1271 he took the dynastic name Great Yuan from the Book of Changes ("Great indeed is the Primal Qian"), and in 1272 Zhongdu was renamed Dadu.
A Central Secretariat ran the government, and branch secretariats (provinces) were set up step by step in the regions; Tibet was governed through the Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs (at first the Supreme Control Commission). After the Battle of Xiangyang (1268–1273), Bayan entered Lin'an in 1276, and the destruction of the Song at Yamen in 1279 unified China. The Yuan emperor was nominally overlord of the four khanates.

大汗兀鲁思.note: The Mongol homeland ruled directly by the Great Khan. Under Genghis Khan it passed to his youngest son, Tolui, as "keeper of the hearth"; Ögedei built his capital, Karakorum, by the Orkhon River.

汉地.note: From 1217 Muqali, as Grand Preceptor and Prince of the State, directed the conquest of North China; after the fall of Jin the Yanjing Branch Secretariat was set up, and hereditary Chinese warlords held the prefectures and counties. In 1251 Möngke put Kublai in charge of all military and civil affairs in the Chinese lands south of the Gobi.

东道诸王.note: The appanages of Genghis Khan's brothers (Qasar, Qachi'un, Temüge Otchigin and Belgütei), on either side of the Greater Khingan, along the Nen River and in Hulunbuir. The line of Temüge Otchigin was the strongest.

术赤兀鲁思.note: The appanage of the eldest son, Jochi, at first on the steppe west of the Irtysh and north of Khwarazm. After Batu's western campaign of the eldest sons (1236–1242) it extended over the Kipchak Steppe and the Volga basin, with its capital at Sarai, and the Rus' principalities paid it tribute. After 1260 it became a state of its own, known as the Golden Horde (the Kipchak Khanate).

察合台兀鲁思.note: The appanage of the second son, Chagatai, in the Ili valley (Almaliq) and Semirechye, with a share of the revenues of the farmlands of Transoxiana. After 1260 it became a state of its own, known as the Chagatai Khanate.

窝阔台兀鲁思.note: The appanage of the third son, Ögedei, at Emil and on the upper Irtysh. Purged and scattered after Möngke's accession, it was rebuilt by Kaidu after the Talas kurultai of 1269 and long fought the Yuan; it is known as the Ögedei Khanate.

阿姆河行省.note: From the 1230s the Great Khan sent officials to govern Khorasan and the Iranian lands west of the Amu Darya (the Branch Secretariat of the Amu Darya and other places), based at Tus. It was absorbed into Hulagu's ulus after his arrival in 1256.

旭烈兀兀鲁思.note: In 1253 Möngke sent his brother Hulagu west. He destroyed the Nizaris in 1256, took Baghdad in 1258, and entered Syria in 1260, where his army was defeated by the Mamluks at Ain Jalut. After 1260 Hulagu ruled independently from Maragheh and Tabriz; the state is known as the Ilkhanate.

腹里.note: The "Central Region" under the direct rule of the Central Secretariat: today's Hebei, Shandong, Shanxi and southern Inner Mongolia, including both capitals, Dadu and Shangdu.

岭北.note: The Mongol homeland, site of Karakorum. Held by Ariq Böke in 1260–1264 and afterwards fought over again and again with Kaidu and Duwa; Lingbei Province was formally established in 1307.

辽阳.note: Liaodong, the Northeast and the north of the Korean peninsula, home of the appanages of the Eastern Princes. Liaoyang Province took shape step by step after 1269 (fixed in 1287).

陕西四川.note: The Shaanxi–Sichuan Province was set up in 1260 with its seat at Jingzhao. It ran the Sichuan front in the war against Song; all of Sichuan passed to the Yuan after Chongqing fell in 1278 and Diaoyu Fortress surrendered in 1279.

云南.note: Kublai conquered Dali in 1253 and kept the Duan family as governors-general of Dali. In 1274 Sayyid Ajjal Shams al-Din established Yunnan Province, with its seat at Zhongqing (Kunming).

河南江北.note: The former Jin lands of Henan south of the Yellow River and the Southern Song lands of Huainan and northern Jinghu, north of the Yangtze. Henan Jiangbei Province took shape step by step after 1276 (fixed in 1291).

江浙.note: The former Southern Song lands of Liangzhe, Jiangdong and Fujian. After Bayan entered Lin'an in 1276 the Jiang-Huai Province was set up; later called Jiangzhe Province, its seat was at Hangzhou.

江西.note: The former Southern Song circuits of Jiangnan West and Guangnan East. Jiangxi Province was set up in 1277 with its seat at Longxing (Nanchang).

湖广.note: The former Southern Song circuits of Jinghu South, Jinghu North and Guangnan West. A Jinghu Province was set up from 1274, later called Huguang Province, with its seat at Tanzhou and later at Ezhou.

燕山府路.note: Set up in 1123 when Song bought back Yanjing (Yanshan Fu) and the six prefectures of Zhuo, Yi, Tan, Shun, Jing and Ji for an annual payment. In the winter of 1125 the Jin army came south and Guo Yaoshi surrendered Yanshan to Jin; Song had held the Yan lands for little more than two years.

开封府界.note: The capital, Kaifeng Fu, and its metropolitan counties, administered directly by Kaifeng Fu and not attached to any circuit (briefly made the Capital Circuit in 1105).

京东路.note: One of the fifteen circuits of the Zhidao era, covering most of today's Shandong and the Xuzhou area of northern Jiangsu. Divided into East and West circuits in 1072.

京东东路.note: Created in 1072 from the Jingdong Circuit, with its seat at Qingzhou; it governed the Qing, Mi, Qi, Deng, Lai, Zi, Wei and Yi prefectures, among others.

京东西路.note: Created in 1072 from the Jingdong Circuit, with its seat at Yunzhou (Dongping Fu); it governed Yingtian Fu and the Yan, Yun, Xu, Cao, Pu, Shan and Ji prefectures, among others.

京西路.note: One of the fifteen circuits of the Zhidao era, covering today's western Henan and northern Hubei. Divided into South and North circuits in 1072.

京西南路.note: Created in 1072 from the Jingxi Circuit, with its seat at Xiangzhou (Xiangyang Fu); it governed the Xiang, Deng, Sui, Jin, Fang, Jun, Ying and Tang prefectures, among others. Under the Southern Song it was the front line against Jin and the Mongols, and Xiangyang was called "the western gate of the realm".

京西北路.note: Created in 1072 from the Jingxi Circuit, with its seat at Henan Fu (the Western Capital, Luoyang); it governed the Western Capital, Yingchang, and the Zheng, Hua, Meng, Cai, Chen, Ying, Ru and Xinyang prefectures, among others.

河北路.note: One of the fifteen circuits of the Zhidao era and the key to the defense against Liao: along the Baigou (Juma) River, Song dug ponds and marshes and planted elms and willows to hold back the Liao cavalry. From 1048 it was divided into four military-commissioner circuits, and in 1072 into East and West circuits.

河北东路.note: Created in 1072 from the Hebei Circuit, with its seat at Daming Fu (the Northern Capital); it governed the Cang, Ying, Mo, Xiong, Ba, De, Bo, Di, Bin, En and Ji prefectures, among others.

河北西路.note: Created in 1072 from the Hebei Circuit, with its seat at Zhending Fu; it governed the Ding, Bao, Yi, Qi, Shen, Zhao, Xing, Ming, Ci, Xiang, Wei and Huai prefectures, among others.

河东路.note: One of the fifteen circuits of the Zhidao era, with its seat at Bingzhou (Taiyuan Fu), covering most of today's Shanxi and the Fu and Lin prefectures of northern Shaanxi. To the north it faced the Liao Western Capital Circuit along the line of Yanmen Pass; to the west it faced Western Xia across the Yellow River.

陕西路.note: One of the fifteen circuits of the Zhidao era, with its seat at Jingzhao Fu, and the main theater of the war against Western Xia. From the Qingli era it was split into four military commands (Qinfeng, Jingyuan, Huanqing and Fuyan); in 1072 the fiscal circuit was divided into the Yongxing Jun and Qinfeng circuits.

永兴军路.note: Created in 1072 from the Shaanxi Circuit, with its seat at Jingzhao Fu (Yongxing Jun). It governed Jingzhao, Hezhong and the Shan, Yan, Fu, Fang, Dan, Tong, Hua, Yao, Bin, Qing and Ning prefectures, among others, and contained the Fuyan and Huanqing military commands.

秦凤路.note: Created in 1072 from the Shaanxi Circuit, with its seat at Qinzhou. It governed Fengxiang and the Qin, Long, Cheng, Feng, Jie, Wei, Jing and Yuan prefectures, together with the Xi, He, Lan, Gong and Min prefectures won in the Xihe campaign.

淮南路.note: One of the fifteen circuits of the Zhidao era, with its seat at Yangzhou, covering the land between the Yangtze and the Huai. Divided into East and West circuits in 1072.

淮南东路.note: Created in 1072 from the Huainan Circuit, with its seat at Yangzhou; it governed the Yang, Chu (楚), Tai, Zhen, Tong, Hai, Si, Bo, Su and Chu (滁) prefectures, among others. Under the Southern Song, when the Huai was the border with Jin and later Yuan, it shielded the Yangtze defenses.

淮南西路.note: Created in 1072 from the Huainan Circuit, with its seat at Shouzhou (moved to Luzhou under the Southern Song); it governed the Shou, Lu, Qi, He, Shu, Hao, Guang and Huang prefectures and Wuwei Jun, among others.

江南路.note: One of the fifteen circuits of the Zhidao era, the former land of the Southern Tang. Divided into East and West circuits in 1023.

江南东路.note: Created in 1023 from the Jiangnan Circuit, with its seat at Jiangning Fu (Jiankang Fu); it governed Jiangning and the Xuan, She, Chi, Rao, Xin and Taiping prefectures, among others.

江南西路.note: Created in 1023 from the Jiangnan Circuit, with its seat at Hongzhou (Longxing Fu); it governed the Hong, Qian, Ji, Yuan, Fu, Yun and Jiang prefectures and Nan'an Jun, Linjiang Jun and Jianchang Jun.

荆湖北路.note: With its seat at Jiangling Fu, it governed Jiangling and the E, Fu, Yue, Li, Ding, Xia, Gui, Chen and Yuan prefectures, among others. Under the Southern Song a large army was stationed at Ezhou, and Ezhou and Xiangyang supported each other.

荆湖南路.note: With its seat at Tanzhou, it governed the Tan, Heng, Dao, Yong, Chen, Shao and Quan prefectures, among others.

两浙路.note: With its seat at Hangzhou, the former land of the Wuyue kingdom and one of the richest circuits of the Northern Song. Divided into East and West circuits early in the Southern Song.

两浙西路.note: Created under the Southern Song from the Liangzhe Circuit, with its seat at Lin'an Fu (the temporary capital); it governed Lin'an, Pingjiang, Zhenjiang and the Hu, Xiu, Chang and Yan prefectures, among others.

两浙东路.note: Created under the Southern Song from the Liangzhe Circuit, with its seat at Shaoxing Fu; it governed Shaoxing, Qingyuan (Mingzhou) and the Wu, Qu, Tai, Wen and Chu prefectures, among others.

福建路.note: With its seat at Fuzhou, it governed the six prefectures of Fu, Jian, Quan, Zhang, Ting and Nanjian and Shaowu Jun and Xinghua Jun. Quanzhou was the greatest port of the Song and Yuan.

西川路.note: One of the fifteen circuits of the Zhidao era, with its seat at Yizhou (Chengdu). In 1001 it and the Xia Circuit were divided into the four circuits of Yi, Zi, Li and Kui (the four Sichuan circuits).

峡路.note: One of the fifteen circuits of the Zhidao era, with its seat at Kuizhou, covering the Three Gorges and eastern Sichuan. Merged into the four Sichuan circuits in 1001.

成都府路.note: One of the four Sichuan circuits, at first called the Yizhou Circuit and renamed the Chengdu Fu Circuit in 1059, with its seat at Chengdu Fu.

梓州路.note: One of the four Sichuan circuits, with its seat at Zizhou (raised to Tongchuan Fu in 1118, when the circuit was renamed the Tongchuan Fu Circuit); it governed the prefectures of central and southern Sichuan.

利州路.note: One of the four Sichuan circuits, with its seat at Xingyuan Fu; it governed Xingyuan and the Li, Yang, Lang, Jian, Wen, Long, Ba, Peng and Ji prefectures, among others, and held the gateways into Sichuan. Under the Southern Song it was several times split into Lizhou East and West circuits and joined again.

夔州路.note: One of the four Sichuan circuits, with its seat at Kuizhou; it governed the prefectures of the Three Gorges, eastern Sichuan and Qianzhong, with many loose-rein prefectures and tribal settlements.

广南东路.note: With its seat at Guangzhou, it covered most of today's Guangdong.

广南西路.note: With its seat at Guizhou (Jingjiang Fu), it covered today's Guangxi and Hainan; the Yongzhou area bordered Đại Việt.

上京道.note: The circuit of the Liao Supreme Capital, Linhuang Fu (today's Bairin Left Banner), the Khitan heartland. It reached north to the Kherlen River and to Zhenzhou (Kedun City) and governed the Zubu tribes.

中京道.note: In 1007 Emperor Shengzong of Liao built the Central Capital, Dading Fu (today's Ningcheng), on the old site of the Xi king's camp; the circuit governed the Xi lands and the prefectures west of the Liao River.

东京道.note: The circuit of the Eastern Capital, Liaoyang Fu, on the former land of Balhae. It reached north to Huanglong Fu and Ningjiang Zhou, governed the tribes of the Civilized Jurchens, and bordered Goryeo along the Yalu River to the east.

南京道.note: The circuit of the Southern Capital, Xijin Fu (Youzhou): the prefectures south of the mountains among the Sixteen Prefectures, the richest Chinese lands of the Liao. Before 1044 the prefectures north of the mountains also belonged to it.

西京道.note: In 1044 Emperor Xingzong of Liao made Yunzhou the Western Capital, Datong Fu; the circuit governed the prefectures north of the mountains and the Feng, Dongsheng, Tiande and Yunnei prefectures, among others, as a bulwark against Xia.

上京路.note: The land where the Jurchens rose, with its seat at Huining Fu (Acheng, Harbin). Huining was made the Supreme Capital in 1138; it lost the title when Wanyan Liang moved the capital to Yanjing, and Emperor Shizong restored it in 1173. Under it were the Puyu, Huligai, Helan and Xupin circuits, among others.

咸平路.note: With its seat at Xianping Fu (today's Kaiyuan).

东京路.note: With its seat at the Eastern Capital, Liaoyang Fu, where many Balhae descendants lived; it bordered Goryeo along the Yalu River to the east.

北京路.note: With its seat at Dading Fu (the former Liao Central Capital), renamed the Northern Capital in 1153; it governed Linhuang Fu and the prefectures of the former Liao Central Capital Circuit.

西京路.note: With its seat at Datong Fu; along its north Jin built border trenches (the Jin "Great Wall") against the steppe tribes.

中都路.note: At first called the Yanjing Circuit; renamed the Zhongdu Circuit when Wanyan Liang moved the capital to Yanjing in 1153, with its seat at Daxing Fu.

南京路.note: With its seat at Kaifeng Fu. Kaifeng was renamed the Southern Capital in 1153, and Emperor Xuanzong of Jin moved the capital there in 1214.

金河北东路.note: With its seat at Hejian Fu.

金河北西路.note: With its seat at Zhending Fu.

大名府路.note: With its seat at Daming Fu.

山东东路.note: With its seat at Yidu Fu (Qingzhou). The Red Coat rebels rose here at the end of the Jin; it was later held by Li Quan and his son Li Tan.

山东西路.note: With its seat at Dongping Fu.

河东北路.note: With its seat at Taiyuan Fu.

河东南路.note: With its seat at Pingyang Fu.

京兆府路.note: With its seat at Jingzhao Fu.

凤翔路.note: With its seat at Fengxiang Fu; to the southwest it faced Song across Dasan Pass.

鄜延路.note: With its seat at Yan'an Fu; it bordered Western Xia to the north.

庆原路.note: With its seat at Qingyang Fu.

临洮路.note: With its seat at Lintao Fu (Xizhou).

吐蕃诸部.note:
After the collapse of the Tibetan Empire in 842 the Tibetan plateau remained divided for centuries: descendants of the royal house held Ngari (Guge), Lhasa and Yarlung, and local magnates and religious schools owed no allegiance to one another. From the 11th century Buddhism revived in the "later diffusion", and the Sakya and Kagyu schools arose.
In 1240 the Mongol prince Köten sent Doorda Darqan into Tibet; in 1247 Sakya Pandita met Köten at Liangzhou, and Tibet submitted to the Mongols. In 1264 Kublai set up the Supreme Control Commission (later the Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs) under Phagpa, and Tibet came formally under Yuan rule.

唃厮啰.note: Around 1032 Gusiluo ("son of the Buddha"), a descendant of the Tibetan emperors, founded a state centered on Qingtang City (today's Xining). Allied with Song against Xia, he crushed Li Yuanhao at Zongge in 1035. The state held Hehuang and controlled the Qinghai branch of the Silk Road. It declined after Gusiluo's death in 1065; Song took Hehuang twice, in 1099 and 1104, and set up the Xining, Huang and Kuo prefectures.

六谷部.note: After the Tibetan collapse at the end of the Tang, the Tibetan and Chinese groups of Liangzhou formed the Six Valleys confederation. Its leader Panluozhi sided with Song against the Tanguts and in 1004 lured Li Jiqian into a trap and shot him. After 1015 Liangzhou was repeatedly fought over by the Ganzhou Uyghurs and the Tanguts, and Li Yuanhao took it in 1032.

甘州回鹘.note: A branch of the Uyghurs who moved south into the Hexi Corridor after the collapse of the Uyghur Khaganate in 840. At the end of the 9th century they founded a khaganate at Ganzhou (today's Zhangye), whose rulers called themselves khagan and sent tribute to the Chinese courts. Destroyed by the Tangut Li Yuanhao in 1028; the remnant moved south and became the Yellow-headed Uyghurs (ancestors of today's Yugurs).

归义军.note: In 848 Zhang Yichao led a rising at Shazhou, and in 851 he brought the region back to Tang allegiance and was made commander of the Guiyi Circuit; later the office was hereditary in the line of Cao Yijin (c. 914–1036). The circuit held the Sha and Gua prefectures and followed the Chinese court calendar. The great hoard of manuscripts in the Dunhuang Library Cave was sealed in this period (c. 1000). Annexed by Western Xia around 1036.

高昌回鹘.note: A branch of the Uyghurs who moved west in 840, with their capital at Qocho (Xizhou) and their summer capital at Beshbaliq; they held the eastern Tian Shan and followed Buddhism and Manichaeism. In the 12th century they were vassals of the Western Liao. In 1209 the idiqut Barchuq Art Tegin killed the Western Liao resident official and submitted to Genghis Khan, who acknowledged him as his "fifth son". Under the Mongols their Chinese name became Weiwu'er; harried by Kaidu and Duwa after the 1270s, the idiqut moved east to Yongchang.

于阗.note: A Buddhist kingdom ruled by the Viśa (Yuchi) family, with its capital at Xicheng (today's Hotan), which claimed a nephew-to-uncle kinship with the Tang. In the late 10th century it fought a long holy war with the Kara-Khanids and was conquered by them around 1006; from then on the southern rim of the Tarim Basin became Muslim.

喀喇汗.note:
A dynasty founded by Karluk, Yaghma and other Turkic tribes. Around the middle of the 10th century Satuq Bughra Khan converted to Islam, making it the first Turkic Muslim dynasty. Its capitals were Balasagun and Kashgar. It took Bukhara in 999, ending the Samanids, and conquered Khotan in 1006.
In the 1040s it split into two khanates: the eastern one held Balasagun, Kashgar and Semirechye, the western one Samarkand and Transoxiana. The eastern khanate lost Balasagun to the Western Liao in 1134 and afterwards held Kashgar as a vassal until Kuchlug destroyed it in 1211. Mahmud al-Kashgari, author of the Compendium of the Turkic Dialects, came from its royal house.

西喀喇汗.note: The western branch of the Kara-Khanids after the split of the 1040s, with its capital at Samarkand, holding Transoxiana and Fergana. It submitted to the Seljuks in 1089 and became a vassal of the Western Liao after the Battle of Qatwan in 1141. It ended in 1212 when Muhammad II, Shah of Khwarazm, killed its last ruler, Uthman.

葛逻禄.note: Turkic tribes living south of Lake Balkhash and in the Ili valley. In the 12th century they held the Qayaliq and Almaliq area as vassals of the Western Liao; in 1211 their leader Arslan Khan submitted to Genghis Khan.

黠戛斯.note: A Turkic-speaking people of the Kem (upper Yenisei), who destroyed the Uyghur Khaganate under the Tang. Called Xiajiasi and Jilijisi in Liao and Jin times, they surrendered to Jochi in 1207, rebelled in 1218 and were subdued again.

萨曼.note: A dynasty founded by the Persian Saman family (819–999), nominally loyal to the Abbasid caliph but in fact ruling Transoxiana and Khorasan from Bukhara. It fostered the revival of Persian literature, patronizing Rudaki and Ferdowsi. At the end of the 10th century its Turkish slave commanders grew too strong; it lost Khorasan to the Ghaznavids in 994, and the dynasty ended when the Kara-Khanids took Bukhara in 999.

伽色尼.note:
In 977 Sebüktigin, a Turkish slave commander of the Samanids, made himself independent at Ghazni. His son Mahmud (998–1030) raided India seventeen times, sacked the temple of Somnath in 1025, and took Khorasan, Khwarazm and Rayy, bringing the dynasty to its height; Ferdowsi presented his Shahnameh at Mahmud's court.
Defeated by the Seljuks at Dandanaqan in 1040, the Ghaznavids lost Khorasan and afterwards held Afghanistan and the Punjab. After the Ghurids sacked Ghazni in 1151 the Ghaznavids moved their capital to Lahore, and the Ghurids destroyed them in 1186.

古尔.note: A Tajik dynasty from the mountains of Ghor in central Afghanistan, with its capital at Firuzkuh (the Minaret of Jam is its relic). In 1151 Ala al-Din "the World-Burner" sacked Ghazni. It reached its height under the brothers Ghiyath al-Din and Muhammad: they took Ghazni in 1173, destroyed the Ghaznavids in 1186, defeated the Rajput coalition at the second Battle of Tarain in 1192 and took Delhi. Muhammad was assassinated in 1206, and his Turkish slave commander Aybak made himself independent at Delhi; the Ghurid homeland was annexed by Khwarazm in 1215.

德里苏丹国.note: In 1206 Qutb al-Din Aybak, a Turkish slave commander of the Ghurids, made himself independent at Delhi, founding the Slave (Mamluk) dynasty. Iltutmish (1211–1236) consolidated the realm and refused to shelter Jalal al-Din so as not to provoke the Mongols; Balban (1266–1287) repeatedly fought off Mongol invasions in the Punjab.

花剌子模.note:
An oasis state on the lower Amu Darya, with its capital at Gurganj. In 1077 the Seljuks appointed the Turkish slave Anushtegin governor, and his descendants held the title Khwarazmshah. After 1141 it was a vassal of the Western Liao. Tekish destroyed the Seljuks of Iraq in 1194; Muhammad II (1200–1220) took Transoxiana (1212) and Ghor (1215), with an empire reaching from Iraq to the Syr Darya, and was hailed as "a second Alexander".
In 1218 the governor of Otrar killed a Mongol caravan, bringing on Genghis Khan's western campaign: Bukhara and Samarkand fell in 1220, and Muhammad died on an island in the Caspian Sea. His son Jalal al-Din fought on along the Indus, in Iran and in Azerbaijan until he died in the Kurdish mountains in 1231, and the state came to an end.

布韦希.note: A Shiite warrior family from the Daylam highlands south of the Caspian, who entered Baghdad in 945 and controlled the Abbasid caliph with the title of Grand Emir. Under Adud al-Dawla (949–983), who united Iraq, Fars and Jibal, it was at its height, with its capital at Shiraz. Afterwards it split and fell to infighting; the Seljuk Tughril entered Baghdad in 1055, and the last regime, in Fars, ended in 1062.

塞尔柱.note:
The Seljuk clan of the Oghuz Turks. In 1037 the brothers Tughril and Chaghri took Nishapur; in 1040 they routed the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan and took Khorasan. Tughril entered Baghdad in 1055 and received the title of sultan from the caliph. Alp Arslan captured the Byzantine emperor at Manzikert in 1071; under Malik-Shah (1072–1092) the empire reached from Kashgar to the Mediterranean, and the vizier Nizam al-Mulk founded the Nizamiyya colleges.
After Malik-Shah's death in 1092 his sons fought a civil war, and the empire split into the branches of Rum, Iraq, Syria and Kerman. Sanjar ruled Khorasan as Great Sultan; he was defeated by the Western Liao at Qatwan in 1141 and captured by Oghuz nomads in 1153, and with his death in 1157 the eastern empire came to an end.

伊拉克塞尔柱.note: From 1118 grandsons of Malik-Shah ruled Iraq and western Iran from Hamadan, nominally under Sanjar of Khorasan as Great Sultan, while real power passed gradually to the atabegs. Independent after 1157; the last sultan, Tughril III, was killed at Rayy in 1194 and the line was destroyed by Khwarazm.

克尔曼塞尔柱.note: A branch founded in 1048 by Qavurt, son of Chaghri, at Kerman, controlling the Persian Gulf trade. It was ended by Oghuz tribes in 1186.

罗姆.note: Founded in Anatolia in 1077, after the Battle of Manzikert, by the Seljuk prince Suleiman, with its first capital at Nicaea; after the First Crusade retook Nicaea in 1097 the capital moved to Konya (Iconium). Rum routed Byzantium at Myriokephalon in 1176 and was at its height under Kayqubad I (1220–1237), when caravanserais spread across Anatolia. Defeated by the Mongols at Köse Dağ in 1243, it became a vassal of the Mongols (later of the Ilkhanate).

达尼什曼德.note: A Turkish dynasty founded after Manzikert in north-central Anatolia (Sivas, Kayseri, Niksar), which captured Bohemond of Antioch in 1100. It long contended with the Sultanate of Rum for supremacy and was swallowed by Rum in 1178.

木剌夷.note: The Nizari branch of the Ismailis. In 1090 Hasan-i Sabbah seized Alamut Castle; from a network of mountain castles in the Alborz, Quhistan and the Syrian highlands they held out and became notorious for assassinating their enemies (the "Assassins"). In 1256 Hulagu took Maymun-Diz, Alamut and the other castles and the last imam, Rukn al-Din, surrendered; he was killed the next year on his way back from Mongolia; Girdkuh held out until 1270.

阿拔斯.note: The Islamic empire founded in 750, with its capital at Baghdad. From the 10th century the caliphs lost real power, controlled first by the Buyids (945–1055) and then by the Seljuks (1055 to the 1150s), and kept only religious authority. As the Seljuks declined, caliphs such as al-Muqtafi and al-Nasir (1180–1225) restored real rule over Iraq. In 1258 Hulagu stormed Baghdad and killed the last caliph, al-Musta'sim, and the Abbasid dynasty came to an end.

法蒂玛.note: A Shiite Ismaili caliphate that rose in North Africa in 909, took Egypt in 969, founded Cairo as its capital and established al-Azhar mosque. In the late 10th century it held Egypt, southern Syria and the Hejaz. It lost Damascus to the Seljuks in the 1070s and Jerusalem to the Crusaders in 1099. In 1171 Saladin deposed the last caliph and the dynasty ended.

赞吉.note: The Seljuk atabeg Imad al-Din Zengi took Mosul in 1127 and Aleppo in 1128, and his capture of Edessa in 1144 began the decline of the Crusader states. His son Nur ad-Din took Damascus in 1154, united Muslim Syria and sent Shirkuh and Saladin into Egypt. After Nur ad-Din's death in 1174 Syria passed to Saladin; the Mosul branch lasted until 1233 and was then ruled by its minister Badr al-Din Lu'lu', who submitted to the Mongols.

贾兹拉诸埃米尔.note: After the decline of the Buyids, Upper Mesopotamia (the Jazira) was divided among Arab and Kurdish emirs: the Kurdish Marwanids held Diyarbakır (990–1085) and the Arab Uqaylids Mosul (990–1096). The Seljuks absorbed them one after another in the 1080s and 1090s.

叙利亚诸埃米尔.note: After the Seljuk empire split in the 1090s, Syria was divided among Seljuk princes and atabegs: Aleppo (Ridwan), Damascus (Duqaq, later the Burid dynasty), Homs, Hama and other city-states fought one another and could not stop the First Crusade. In the mid-12th century they were absorbed one by one into the Zengid state.

阿尤布.note:
The Kurd Saladin became vizier of Egypt in 1169, deposed the Fatimid caliph in 1171 and founded the Ayyubid dynasty. In 1174–1186 he took Damascus, Aleppo, Mosul and other lands; in 1187 he routed the Crusaders at Hattin and retook Jerusalem; in 1191–1192 he faced Richard the Lionheart and made the Treaty of Jaffa.
After Saladin's death his sons and nephews divided Cairo, Damascus, Aleppo, Hama and the Jazira, with the sultan of Egypt as overlord. In 1229 al-Kamil made a treaty with Frederick II returning Jerusalem. In 1250 the Egyptian regime was seized by the Mamluks, and the Syrian branches fell to the Mongols and Mamluks in 1260.

马穆鲁克.note: The Turkish slave guard of the Ayyubids. In 1250 they captured King Louis IX of France at Mansurah, killed Sultan Turanshah the same year and seized Egypt. In 1260 Qutuz and Baybars routed the Mongols at Ain Jalut, stopping the Mongol advance west, and then took Syria. Baybars (1260–1277) re-established the Abbasid caliphate in Cairo and repeatedly attacked the Crusader castles (taking Antioch in 1268 and Krak des Chevaliers in 1271).

十字军诸国.note: In 1095 Pope Urban II called the First Crusade. The crusaders took Edessa and Antioch in 1098 and Jerusalem in 1099, and founded four Latin states in the Levant: the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the Principality of Antioch, the County of Tripoli and the County of Edessa. Zengi took Edessa in 1144; Jerusalem was lost after Hattin in 1187, and the Third Crusade (1189–1192) recovered Acre and other coastal cities. Antioch fell to the Mamluks in 1268, and with the fall of Acre in 1291 the Crusader states came to an end.

耶路撒冷王国.note: Founded after Godfrey of Bouillon took Jerusalem in 1099; his brother Baldwin I took the title of king in 1100. After Hattin in 1187 it lost Jerusalem, and from 1191 its capital was Acre, so that it is also called the "Kingdom of Acre". It briefly regained Jerusalem in 1229–1244.

安条克公国.note: Founded after Bohemond of Taranto took Antioch in 1098, it long contended with Byzantium and Aleppo. It became a Mongol dependency in the 1260s and was destroyed by the Mamluk sultan Baybars in 1268.

塞浦路斯王国.note: Richard the Lionheart seized Cyprus on his way east in 1191 and the next year sold it to Guy of Lusignan, former king of Jerusalem; it became a kingdom in 1197 and served as the rear base of the Crusader states in the eastern Mediterranean.

的黎波里伯国.note: Founded after the son of Count Raymond of Toulouse took Tripoli in 1109; it held Krak des Chevaliers (handed to the Knights Hospitaller in 1142). Destroyed by the Mamluks in 1289.

埃德萨伯国.note: The first Crusader state, founded on the Euphrates by Baldwin of Boulogne in 1098. Zengi took Edessa in 1144, and the county was lost entirely in 1150.

小亚美尼亚.note: After the Seljuk invasions Armenians moved south into Cilicia, where the Rubenid family founded a principality in 1080; in 1198 Leo I was crowned king by the Holy Roman Emperor, with his capital at Sis. The kingdom allied with the Crusaders through marriage, and Hethum I went in person to Karakorum in 1254 to pay court to Möngke and win Mongol support.

亚美尼亚.note: The Bagratid dynasty, with its capital at Ani ("city of a thousand churches"). Annexed by Byzantium in 1045; Ani was taken by the Seljuk Alp Arslan in 1064.

格鲁吉亚.note: The Bagrationi dynasty united eastern and western Georgia in 1008. David IV "the Builder" routed the Seljuk coalition at Didgori in 1121 and retook Tbilisi as his capital in 1122; under Queen Tamar (1184–1213) Georgia dominated the Caucasus and sponsored the Empire of Trebizond. Invaded by Subutai and then by Jalal al-Din in the 1220s, it submitted to the Mongols after 1236.

希尔万.note: The Shirvanshahs on the western shore of the Caspian, with their capital at Shamakhi, controlled the pass of Derbent. They acknowledged in turn the Seljuks, Georgia and the Mongols as overlords, and the dynasty lasted for centuries.

阿塞拜疆阿塔贝格.note: Eldiguz, atabeg of the Seljuks of Iraq, held Azerbaijan and Arran from 1136; his line served for generations as regents of the Seljuk sultans, with their capital at Tabriz. Independent after the fall of the Seljuks in 1194, they were destroyed by Jalal al-Din in 1225.

萨尔古尔.note: Atabegs of the Oghuz Salghur tribe, who held Fars (Shiraz) from 1148, submitting in turn to the Seljuks and to Khwarazm. In the 1230s they submitted to the Mongols of their own accord and so spared Shiraz; the poet Saadi lived under this dynasty.

拜占庭.note:
The Eastern Roman Empire, with its capital at Constantinople. Basil II "the Bulgar-Slayer" (976–1025) crushed Bulgaria at Kleidion in 1014, annexed the whole country by 1018, and also annexed the Armenian lands of Tao and Vaspurakan. In 1071 Romanos IV was captured by the Seljuks at Manzikert and the Anatolian interior was lost; in the same year Bari fell and Byzantium withdrew from Italy.
The Komnenian dynasty (1081–1185) used the Crusades to recover western Anatolia. In 1204 the Fourth Crusade took Constantinople and the empire broke up into Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond; in 1261 Michael VIII of Nicaea recovered Constantinople and the empire was restored.

拉丁帝国.note: Founded after the Fourth Crusade took Constantinople in 1204, with Count Baldwin of Flanders as emperor; Venice received over a third of the territory. Crushed by the Bulgarians at Adrianople in 1205, it shrank steadily afterwards and was destroyed by the Empire of Nicaea in 1261.

特拉比松.note: Founded at Trebizond in 1204 by the Komnenos brothers Alexios and David with the support of Queen Tamar of Georgia, it controlled the trade routes of the southeastern Black Sea coast and submitted to the Mongols after 1243.

伊庇鲁斯.note: A Byzantine successor state founded in northwestern Greece in 1205 by the nobleman Michael Komnenos Doukas, with its capital at Arta. In 1224 it briefly took Thessalonica and claimed the imperial title, contending with Nicaea for legitimacy.

保加利亚.note: The First Bulgarian Empire under Tsar Samuel (997–1014), with its capital at Ohrid, fought Byzantium for decades; crushed at Kleidion in 1014, it fell in 1018. In 1185 the brothers Asen and Peter rose and founded the Second Bulgarian Empire, with its capital at Tarnovo; in 1205 it captured the Latin emperor Baldwin at Adrianople, and under Ivan Asen II (1218–1241) it dominated the Balkans. After 1242 it paid tribute to the Golden Horde.

塞尔维亚.note: The Grand Principality of Raška, long subject to Byzantium. Stefan Nemanja (1166–1196) united the Serbian lands; his son Stefan was crowned king by the pope in 1217, and Sava established an autocephalous Serbian Church in 1219.

克罗地亚.note: The Kingdom of Croatia entered a personal union with Hungary in 1102 (the Pacta conventa), after which the king of Hungary was also king of Croatia.

匈牙利.note: The Magyars entered the Carpathian Basin at the end of the 9th century. Saint Stephen was crowned king in 1000 and converted to Catholicism, with his capital at Esztergom. Hungary acquired Croatia in 1102. In 1241 its army was annihilated by Batu and Subutai at Mohi on the Sajó; Béla IV fled to an island off Dalmatia, and after the Mongols withdrew the next year he rebuilt the kingdom and raised stone castles everywhere.

波兰.note: The Piast dynasty: Mieszko I was baptized in 966 and Bolesław I crowned king in 1025. In 1138 the will of Bolesław III "Wrymouth" divided the country, which then remained fragmented for nearly two centuries (Greater Poland, Lesser Poland, Silesia, Masovia and other duchies). In the Mongol invasion of 1241 Kraków was burned and Duke Henry II of Silesia fell at Legnica.

神圣罗马帝国.note: Otto I was crowned in 962 and claimed to continue the Roman Empire. This map shows only its southeastern part: Bohemia (a kingdom from 1198) and Austria (a duchy from 1156). In 1241 Mongol raiders reached the area of Wiener Neustadt.

波希米亚.note: The duchy of the Přemyslid dynasty; Ottokar I took the title of king in 1198, with his capital at Prague.

奥地利.note: The march of the Babenberg family, raised to a duchy in 1156, with its capital at Vienna. When the line died out in 1246 it passed to Ottokar II, king of Bohemia.

威尼斯.note: The merchant republic of the Adriatic. In the Fourth Crusade it gained Crete (ruled directly from 1211) and other footholds in the eastern Mediterranean.

西西里.note: The Norman Robert Guiscard took Bari in 1071, the last Byzantine stronghold in Italy; his brother Roger I took Sicily in 1091. Roger II became king of Sicily in 1130, with his capital at Palermo. The kingdom passed to the Hohenstaufen Henry VI in 1194, and his son Frederick II succeeded in 1198; it was seized by Charles of Anjou in 1266.

条顿骑士团.note: A German military order founded before Acre in 1190. Invited by the duke of Masovia in 1226 to fight the Prussians, it built Toruń in 1231 and Königsberg in 1255; absorbing the Livonian Brothers of the Sword in 1237, it gained Livonia (Riga). In 1242 it was defeated by Alexander Nevsky of Novgorod in the Battle on the Ice on Lake Peipus.

立陶宛.note: The Lithuanians, one of the Baltic peoples, were united by Mindaugas in the 1230s; he was baptized and crowned king in 1253, and resisted the Teutonic Order and the Mongols.

罗斯.note:
The state of the Eastern Slavs under the Rurikid dynasty, with its capital at Kyiv. Grand Prince Volodymyr was baptized into Orthodox Christianity in 988, and Yaroslav the Wise (1019–1054) issued the Russkaya Pravda. The Council of Liubech in 1097 recognized the princes' hereditary lands; after Mstislav's death in 1132 the state broke up into more than ten principalities (the Rus' principalities), among which Vladimir-Suzdal, Novgorod and Galicia–Volhynia rose to prominence.
In 1223 a Rus'–Kipchak army was defeated by Jebe and Subutai at the Kalka River. In Batu's campaign of 1237–1240 Ryazan, Vladimir and Kyiv were burned one after another; the Rus' principalities had to pay tribute to the Golden Horde and receive their princes' patents from the khan (the "Tatar yoke").

弗拉基米尔.note: A principality in northeastern Rus'. The name of Moscow first appears under Yuri Dolgoruky in 1147; Andrei Bogolyubsky moved the capital to Vladimir in 1157 and sacked Kyiv in 1169. Batu destroyed it in 1238, and Grand Prince Yuri II fell at the Sit River.

诺夫哥罗德.note: The merchant republic of northwestern Rus', whose town assembly (veche) chose and hired its princes; a hub of the Hanseatic trade. The Mongols never reached its walls, but it had to pay tribute. It defeated the Swedes on the Neva in 1240 and the Teutonic Order on Lake Peipus in 1242.

基辅公国.note: The old capital of Rus', sacked by rival princes in 1169 and 1203 and in steady decline. In December 1240 Batu stormed it and massacred its people.

切尔尼戈夫.note: A principality on the left bank of the Dnieper, hereditary in the line of Oleg; taken by the Mongols in 1239. Prince Igor of Novhorod-Siverskyi, whose campaign against the Kipchaks in 1185 is told in the Tale of Igor's Campaign, belonged to this line.

梁赞.note: A principality on the Oka, the first to face Batu's army in the winter of 1237; the city was stormed and its people massacred, and Grand Prince Yuri was killed.

斯摩棱斯克.note: A principality on the upper Dnieper, controlling the route "from the Varangians to the Greeks".

波洛茨克.note: A principality on the Western Dvina that broke away from Kyiv early and came under Lithuanian influence from the 13th century onward.

加利奇沃伦.note: A principality in southwestern Rus'; Roman Mstislavich united Halych and Volhynia in 1199. His son Danylo was crowned "King of Rus'" by the pope in 1253 but still had to submit to the Golden Horde.

伏尔加保加尔.note: A Turkic Muslim state at the confluence of the Volga and Kama, with its capital at Bolghar, visited by the Abbasid envoy Ibn Fadlan in 922. It controlled the northern fur trade. In 1223 it ambushed the Mongol army returning from the west; Batu destroyed it in 1236.

佩切涅格.note: Turkic nomads who in the 10th century held the steppe of the lower Dnieper and Danube and repeatedly raided Kyiv and Byzantium. Defeated by Yaroslav the Wise before Kyiv in 1036, they were annihilated by Byzantium and the Cumans at Levounion in 1091.

乌古斯.note: The Oghuz (Ghuzz) Turkic tribal confederation, which in the 10th century roamed from the Aral Sea to the lower Volga; its leader bore the title yabghu and wintered at Yangikent. The Seljuks came from one of its branches. Driven out by the Kipchaks in the mid-11th century, those who moved west were called the Torks.

钦察.note: The Turkic Kipchak tribes moved west from the Irtysh in the mid-11th century and displaced the Oghuz and Pechenegs, taking the great steppe from the Irtysh to the Danube (the "Kipchak Steppe"). The Rus' called them Polovtsians and the Byzantines Cumans. Defeated with the Rus' at the Kalka River in 1223, they were conquered by Batu in 1237–1241, and some fled into Hungary.

阿兰.note: An Iranian-speaking people of the northern Caucasus, Orthodox Christians intermarried with the Georgian royal house. In 1222 they joined the Kipchaks against Jebe and Subutai; their capital, Magas, fell to the Mongols in 1239, and their warriors were enrolled in the Mongol army (the Asud Guard of the Yuan).

阻卜.note: The Liao name for the tribes of the Mongolian steppe north of the Gobi (the Song called them Tatars), including the later Keraites, Merkits and Tatars. Liao controlled them through the Northwestern Pacification Office at Kedun City; they were Liao dependents who rebelled and submitted by turns (the revolt of Mogusi, 1092–1100). After the fall of Liao they were independent tribes again; in 1124 Yelü Dashi gathered the "seven prefectures and eighteen tribes" here.

乌古敌烈.note: The Wugu and Dilie tribes, who in Liao times roamed Hulunbuir and the lower Kherlen; Liao ruled them directly through the Wugu-Dilie Military Command. After 1122 they passed to the Jin Northeastern Pacification Office.

克烈.note: A powerful tribe of the central steppe on the Tuul and Orkhon rivers, followers of the Church of the East. Its chief Toghrul received the title Ong Khan from Jin and was once Temüjin's sworn father; Temüjin destroyed the tribe at the Jeje'er Heights in 1203.

乃蛮.note: A powerful tribe between the Altai and Khangai mountains, culturally influenced by the Uyghurs and followers of the Church of the East. Temüjin destroyed it at Naqu Cliff in 1204; Tayang Khan was killed, and his son Kuchlug fled to the Western Liao.

蔑儿乞.note: A tribe on the lower Selenge that once carried off Temüjin's wife Börte. Broken by Temüjin between 1204 and 1208, its remnants fled west and were destroyed by Subutai in 1218.

塔塔儿.note: A powerful tribe around Lake Hulun and Lake Buir that joined Jin against the Mongols and poisoned Temüjin's father, Yesügei. In 1196 Jin, Temüjin and the Ong Khan attacked them together on the Ulja River, and in 1202 Temüjin massacred them.

蒙古部.note: Descendants of the Mengwu Shiwei who moved west from the Ergune River, roaming the upper Onon and Kherlen and the area of Burkhan Khaldun. In the 12th century Qabul and Ambaghai were khans in turn, in blood feud with Jin and the Tatars. Temüjin of the Borjigin was raised as khan of the Kiyad around 1189 and then absorbed the other tribes.

汪古.note: A Turkic-speaking tribe north of the Yin Mountains, followers of the Church of the East, who for generations guarded the Jin border trenches. Its chief Ala-qush submitted to Temüjin in 1204, and the tribe thereafter intermarried with the family of Genghis Khan.

弘吉剌.note: A tribe on the western slopes of the Greater Khingan, east of Lake Buir, famous for its beautiful women and the Mongols' "consort clan": Temüjin's wife Börte came from it.

斡亦剌.note: A forest people of the Eight Rivers region on the upper Yenisei (ancestors of today's Oirat Mongols), who submitted to Jochi in 1207.

室韦.note: Tribes on both sides of the Greater Khingan and along the Nen and Ergune rivers, of common origin with the Khitans. Liao and then Jin made them dependents; one branch, the Mengwu Shiwei, moved west and became the ancestors of the Mongol tribe. After 1214 they passed to the Eastern Princes of the Mongols.

女真.note: Descendants of the Heishui Mohe. Those whom Liao moved south and registered were called the Civilized Jurchens, the unregistered the Wild Jurchens; the Wild Jurchens were a Liao dependency whose chief held the Liao title of military governor of the Wild Jurchen tribes. The Wanyan clan of the Wild Jurchens united the tribes at the end of the 11th century, and in 1114 Aguda rose against Liao.

定安国.note: A state founded by Balhae descendants on the middle Yalu, which sent envoys to Song in the 970s and 980s; destroyed by Liao around 986.

高丽.note:
Founded by Wang Geon in 918, with its capital at Gaegyeong (today's Kaesong); it united the Korean peninsula in 936. Invaded three times by Liao, in 993, 1010 and 1018, it won the great victory at Gwiju under Gang Gam-chan in 1019 and afterwards followed the Liao calendar. In 1107 Yun Gwan built nine forts to the north against the Jurchens, which were soon returned; in 1126 Goryeo submitted to Jin.
In the military coup of 1170 the generals took power, and the Choe family ruled for sixty years. From 1231 the Mongols invaded six times; the court moved to Ganghwa Island to resist, the crown prince went to the Mongol court to surrender in 1259, and the court returned to Gaegyeong in 1270, while the Sambyeolcho fell back to Jindo and Jeju (suppressed in 1273). Goryeo was thereafter a Yuan vassal, and in 1274 it joined the Yuan invasion of Japan.

日本.note: In the late Heian period the Fujiwara regency reached its height under Fujiwara no Michinaga (966–1027); from 1086 the retired emperor Shirakawa began rule by cloistered emperors. In the Genpei War of 1180–1185 the Taira were destroyed at Dan-no-ura in 1185; in 1192 Minamoto no Yoritomo became shogun and founded the Kamakura shogunate, and after the Jōkyū War of 1221 the Hōjō ruled as regents. In 1274 a Yuan–Goryeo force invaded (the Bun'ei campaign), landed at Hakata Bay and withdrew.

大理.note: Founded by Duan Siping in 937, with its capital at Yangjumie City (the old town of Dali). The kingdom was devoutly Buddhist; Emperor Taizu of Song "drew the border along the Dadu River with a jade axe", and Song bought horses from Dali at the Hengshan Fort market in Yongzhou. In 1094 the powerful minister Gao Shengtai usurped the throne (as the Great Zhong kingdom), but in 1096 returned it to the Duan (the Later Dali), and the Gao family held the chief ministry for generations. Kublai conquered it in 1253 after "crossing the river on skin rafts"; the Duan family became governors-general of Dali, a post they held until the end of the Yuan.

大越.note: In 968 Đinh Bộ Lĩnh put down the Twelve Warlords and founded Đại Cồ Việt, with its capital at Hoa Lư. Lê Hoàn usurped the throne in 980 (the Early Lê dynasty) and drove back the Song army at the Bạch Đằng River the next year. Lý Công Uẩn founded the Lý dynasty in 1009 and moved the capital to Thăng Long (today's Hanoi) in 1010; the state took the name Đại Việt in 1054. In 1075–1077 Lý Thường Kiệt attacked Yongzhou in Song territory, and the Song general Guo Kui counterattacked as far as the Phú Lương River before withdrawing. The Trần replaced the Lý in 1225 and drove back Uriyangkhadai in 1257–1258.

占城.note: The Cham kingdom of Champa, with its capital at Indrapura (today's Đà Nẵng), moved its capital to Vijaya (today's Gia Lai) in 1000. It fought Đại Việt and the Khmer for centuries, and in 1177 its navy sailed up the Mekong and took Angkor. Annexed by the Khmer in 1203–1220, it later regained independence.

真腊.note: The Angkorian dynasty of the Khmers, with its capital at Yasodharapura (Angkor). Suryavarman II (1113–1150) built Angkor Wat; after Champa took the capital in 1177, Jayavarman VII restored the kingdom, built Angkor Thom and the Bayon, and annexed Champa in 1203.

蒲甘.note: Anawrahta united Burma in 1044, with his capital at Pagan; the kingdom followed Theravada Buddhism and built thousands of temples and stupas. Defeated by the Yuan at Ngasaunggyan in 1277; Pagan fell in 1287.

泥婆罗.note: The kingdom of the Kathmandu Valley, in close contact with Tibet. In 1260 the craftsman Araniko came to the Yuan court with Phagpa and directed the building of the White Stupa in Dadu.
